name: Colonic Interposition
overview: Colon graft for esophageal replacement when stomach unavailable

pimpingQuestions.question: Which colonic segment is most commonly used for esophageal replacement, and what embryologic blood supply makes it suitable?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Left colon (descending/transverse) based on the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from IMA) is most commonly used. The marginal artery provides a reliable arcade. Right colon on the ileocolic pedicle is an alternative. Isoperistaltic placement (proximal colon anastomosed to esophagus) matches normal motility direction.

pimpingQuestions.question: What preoperative study is essential before harvesting colon for interposition?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Mesenteric angiography or CT angiography to confirm the adequacy of the vascular arcade (marginal artery) and identify anatomic variants. Colonoscopy to exclude intrinsic colonic disease. An inadequate marginal artery or colonic pathology is a contraindication.

pimpingQuestions.question: The interposed colon segment has three anastomoses. What are they and which has the highest leak rate?
pimpingQuestions.answer: 1) Cervical esophago-colonic (highest leak rate — 10-20% — due to tension and precarious blood supply at the tip), 2) Colo-gastric or colo-jejunal (distal), 3) Colo-colonic (restoring GI continuity). The cervical anastomosis leaks most because the conduit tip has the most tenuous perfusion.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the most common late complication of colonic interposition?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Redundancy of the interposed segment causing dysphagia, regurgitation, and food stasis as the colon dilates over years. Unlike the stomach, the colon is not designed for peristaltic bolus transport. May require surgical tailoring (colonic plication or replacement).

pimpingQuestions.question: When is colonic interposition preferred over gastric pull-up?
pimpingQuestions.answer: When the stomach is unavailable (prior gastrectomy, gastric cancer), caustic injury involving both esophagus and stomach, or when the stomach's blood supply is compromised. Also preferred in children with long-gap esophageal atresia because the colon grows with the child and has a more reliable long-term conduit.
